# Abstract

Do stronger teams win, and does playing at home still matter? We fit logistic
regression models to `r format(5805, big.mark = ",")` NFL games from the 2000--2021
seasons using FiveThirtyEight's Elo ratings.

Elo rating difference is a powerful predictor: a 100-point Elo edge multiplies the
odds of winning by roughly 1.70. Home-field advantage is also **strongly
significant** --- home teams win about 58% of games between evenly rated opponents,
an edge worth roughly 60 Elo points.

That last result reverses the conclusion of our earlier draft, which found home field
insignificant. The earlier specification compared home games against *neutral-site*
games; because only 61 of 5,866 games are played at neutral sites, that comparison had
almost no statistical power and did not measure home-field advantage at all. The
corrected specification estimates the effect from the model intercept and finds it
highly significant ($p < 10^{-23}$).

We also find that this advantage **collapsed at the end of the study period**. Home
teams won 58.2% of evenly matched games through 2018, but only 51.6% in 2019, 49.3% in
the crowd-free 2020 season, and 50.7% in 2021 (likelihood-ratio test $p = 0.0018$).
On held-out seasons the model over-predicts home wins by 3.8 percentage points, and
this miscalibration is itself a symptom of the decline.

# Introduction

Predicting NFL outcomes attracts fans, analysts and betting markets alike. Conventional
wisdom offers two claims: better teams win, and home field matters. Both are testable.

The Elo rating system, developed by Arpad Elo for chess, assigns each team a single
number that rises after wins and falls after losses, with the size of the adjustment
depending on the result's surprisingness. FiveThirtyEight maintains Elo ratings for
every NFL team back to 1920, updating after each game based on the result, margin of
victory and location.

Home-field advantage is widely documented across sports and attributed to crowd
support, facility familiarity, reduced travel fatigue and referee bias. NFL home teams
have historically won roughly 57--58% of games. The question is whether that edge
survives once we control for the fact that home teams are sometimes simply the better
team.

## Research question

> Does home-field advantage significantly affect the probability of winning an NFL
> game after controlling for team strength, and has its magnitude changed over time?

## A note on the corrected specification

An earlier version of this analysis modelled

$$\text{logit}\left(P(\text{home win})\right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \,\text{EloDiff} + \beta_2 \,\text{HomeGame}$$

where `HomeGame = 1` for home games and `0` for neutral sites. That coefficient
$\beta_2$ contrasts home games with neutral-site games, not home games with away games.
Since the dataset codes `team1` as the home team, *every* non-neutral game has
`HomeGame = 1`; the comparison group is 61 Super Bowls and international games. We
demonstrate the consequences of this in Section \ref{sec-models} and then correct it.

# Data

## Source

FiveThirtyEight's NFL Elo dataset, published under a Creative Commons licence at
<https://github.com/fivethirtyeight/data/tree/master/nfl-elo>. Each row is one game.
The file bundled with this project is a static snapshot; FiveThirtyEight stopped
updating the series after the 2021 season.

```{r load-data}
nfl_raw <- read_csv("data/nfl_elo.csv", show_col_types = FALSE, progress = FALSE)

season_min <- min(nfl_raw$season)
season_max <- max(nfl_raw$season)
```

The snapshot covers `r season_min`--`r season_max` and contains
`r format(nrow(nfl_raw), big.mark = ",")` games.

## Variables

| Variable | Role | Type | Definition |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| `home_win` | Response | Binary | 1 if the home team won, 0 otherwise |
| `elo_diff` | Predictor | Continuous | `elo1_pre - elo2_pre` (home minus away, pre-game) |
| `season` | Predictor / split | Integer | NFL season |
| `neutral` | Filter | Binary | 1 if played at a neutral site |

`elo_diff` is measured *before* the game, so the model uses only information available
at kickoff. Positive values mean the home team is the stronger side.

## Sample construction

```{r sample-construction}
games <- nfl_raw %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(score1), !is.na(score2),   # completed games only
    score1 != score2,                 # ties cannot be modelled as binary win/loss
    season >= 2000                    # modern era
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    home_win   = as.integer(score1 > score2),
    elo_diff   = elo1_pre - elo2_pre,
    point_diff = score1 - score2,
    is_neutral = as.integer(neutral == 1)
  )

# The analytic sample: true home games, where "home advantage" is defined.
games_home <- games %>% filter(is_neutral == 0)
```

```{r sample-table, echo=FALSE}
n_all      <- nrow(nfl_raw)
n_2000     <- nrow(filter(nfl_raw, season >= 2000, !is.na(score1), !is.na(score2)))
n_no_ties  <- nrow(games)
n_neutral  <- sum(games$is_neutral)
n_analytic <- nrow(games_home)

tibble(
  Step = c("Games in snapshot",
           paste0("Completed games, ", 2000, "-", season_max),
           "After removing ties",
           "Neutral-site games removed",
           "Analytic sample (home games)"),
  Games = c(n_all, n_2000, n_no_ties, -n_neutral, n_analytic)
) %>%
  mutate(Games = ifelse(Games < 0,
                        paste0("-", format(abs(Games), big.mark = ",")),
                        format(Games, big.mark = ","))) %>%
  kable(booktabs = TRUE, align = "lr",
        caption = "Sample construction. Each row is a filtering step.") %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = "HOLD_position", font_size = 10) %>%
  row_spec(5, bold = TRUE)
```

Only `r n_neutral` of `r format(n_no_ties, big.mark = ",")` games are played at neutral
sites --- `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * n_neutral / n_no_ties)` of the sample. This is the
crux of the specification problem described above.

# Exploratory analysis

```{r fig-eda, fig.height=3.6, fig.cap="Elo differences cluster near zero, and the home win rate rises monotonically across the Elo range. Bars in the right panel are 95\\% Wilson intervals."}
wilson_ci <- function(x, n, z = 1.96) {
  p      <- x / n
  denom  <- 1 + z^2 / n
  centre <- (p + z^2 / (2 * n)) / denom
  half   <- z * sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n + z^2 / (4 * n^2)) / denom
  tibble(lo = pmax(0, centre - half), hi = pmin(1, centre + half))
}

binned <- games_home %>%
  mutate(bin = cut(elo_diff, breaks = seq(-400, 400, 50))) %>%
  group_by(bin) %>%
  filter(n() >= 30) %>%
  summarise(mid = mean(elo_diff), n = n(), wins = sum(home_win), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(rate = wins / n) %>%
  bind_cols(wilson_ci(.$wins, .$n))

p_left <- ggplot(games_home, aes(elo_diff)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 25, fill = navy, colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = accent, linewidth = 0.6, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "Most games are close matchups",
       subtitle = "Distribution of pre-game Elo difference",
       x = "Elo difference (home \u2212 away)", y = "Games")

p_right <- ggplot(binned, aes(mid, rate)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, colour = grey, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), width = 0, colour = grey, linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(aes(size = n), colour = navy) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 4.5, guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(title = "Stronger teams win more often",
       subtitle = "Observed home win rate by Elo difference",
       x = "Elo difference (home \u2212 away)", y = "Home win rate")

p_left + p_right
```

```{r summary-stats, echo=FALSE}
tibble(
  Statistic = c("Games", "Home win rate", "Mean Elo difference",
                "Median Elo difference", "SD of Elo difference",
                "Elo difference range"),
  Value = c(
    format(n_analytic, big.mark = ","),
    sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * mean(games_home$home_win)),
    sprintf("%+.1f", mean(games_home$elo_diff)),
    sprintf("%+.1f", median(games_home$elo_diff)),
    sprintf("%.1f", sd(games_home$elo_diff)),
    sprintf("%.0f to %+.0f", min(games_home$elo_diff), max(games_home$elo_diff))
  )
) %>%
  kable(booktabs = TRUE, align = "lr",
        caption = "Summary statistics for the analytic sample.") %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = "HOLD_position", font_size = 10)
```

The mean Elo difference is close to zero, confirming that the schedule pits broadly
comparable teams against each other. The home win rate of
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * mean(games_home$home_win))` is the raw, unadjusted figure ---
it conflates home advantage with any tendency for stronger teams to be at home.

## Checking the linearity assumption

Logistic regression assumes the log-odds of the outcome are linear in the predictor.
We can check this directly by plotting the empirical logit of each Elo bin.

```{r fig-logit, fig.height=3.4, fig.cap="The empirical log-odds of a home win are close to linear in Elo difference, supporting the logistic specification."}
emp_logit <- binned %>%
  mutate(logit = log((rate + 0.001) / (1 - rate + 0.001)))

r_lin <- cor(emp_logit$mid, emp_logit$logit)

ggplot(emp_logit, aes(mid, logit)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = accent,
              linewidth = 0.7, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(aes(size = n), colour = navy) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 4.5, guide = "none") +
  annotate("text", x = -330, y = 2.1, hjust = 0, size = 3.4, colour = "grey30",
           label = sprintf("r = %.3f", r_lin)) +
  labs(title = "Log-odds are linear in Elo difference",
       subtitle = "Empirical logit per 50-point Elo bin, with least-squares fit",
       x = "Elo difference (home \u2212 away)", y = "Empirical log-odds of home win",
       caption = "Bins with fewer than 30 games are excluded. Point size is proportional to bin size.")
```

The correlation of `r sprintf("%.3f", r_lin)` between bin midpoint and empirical logit
indicates the linear-in-log-odds assumption is well satisfied. No transformation or
spline term is needed.

# Models {#sec-models}

## Model 1: the flawed specification

We first reproduce the earlier specification to show precisely how it fails.

```{r model-naive}
# Reproduces the original coding exactly: neutral sites are the reference level.
games <- games %>%
  mutate(home_game = factor(ifelse(is_neutral == 0, 1, 0),
                            labels = c("Neutral", "Home")))

m_naive <- glm(home_win ~ elo_diff + home_game, data = games, family = binomial)
```

```{r model-naive-table, echo=FALSE}
broom_like <- function(model, labels) {
  s <- summary(model)$coefficients
  tibble(
    Term        = labels,
    Estimate    = s[, 1],
    `Std. error`= s[, 2],
    `z`         = s[, 3],
    `p-value`   = s[, 4]
  )
}

broom_like(m_naive, c("Intercept (neutral site)", "Elo difference", "Home game")) %>%
  mutate(
    Estimate     = sprintf("%.6f", Estimate),
    `Std. error` = sprintf("%.6f", `Std. error`),
    z            = sprintf("%.2f", z),
    `p-value`    = ifelse(`p-value` < 0.001, "< 0.001", sprintf("%.3f", `p-value`))
  ) %>%
  kable(booktabs = TRUE, align = "lrrrr",
        caption = "Model 1 (flawed). The neutral-site term is estimated from only 61 games.") %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = "HOLD_position", font_size = 10)
```

The location term is insignificant, which the earlier draft read as "home-field
advantage does not matter." But its standard error is roughly ten times the size of the
coefficient, because the comparison group contains `r n_neutral` games. The test is
underpowered by construction, and neutral-site games are unrepresentative anyway: they
are mostly Super Bowls, which are deliberately even matchups between elite teams.

Crucially, this model already contains the answer. Because `team1` is the home team,
the fitted probability at `elo_diff = 0` for an ordinary home game is
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * plogis(coef(m_naive)[1] + coef(m_naive)[3]))` --- the
home-field advantage was there all along, just distributed across the intercept and the
location term rather than isolated in a single testable coefficient.

## Model 2: the corrected specification

Restricting to true home games, home-field advantage *is* the intercept: the log-odds
that the home team wins when the two teams are equally rated.

$$\text{logit}\left(P(\text{home win})\right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \,\text{EloDiff}$$

Here $\beta_0$ is the home-field advantage on the log-odds scale and $\beta_1$ is the
value of one Elo point.

```{r model-final}
m_full <- glm(home_win ~ elo_diff, data = games_home, family = binomial)
```

```{r model-final-table, echo=FALSE}
ci_full <- suppressMessages(confint(m_full))

broom_like(m_full, c("Intercept (home-field advantage)", "Elo difference")) %>%
  mutate(
    `Odds ratio` = sprintf("%.4f", exp(Estimate)),
    Estimate     = sprintf("%.6f", Estimate),
    `Std. error` = sprintf("%.6f", `Std. error`),
    z            = sprintf("%.2f", z),
    `p-value`    = ifelse(`p-value` < 0.001, "< 0.001", sprintf("%.3f", `p-value`))
  ) %>%
  select(Term, Estimate, `Std. error`, z, `p-value`, `Odds ratio`) %>%
  kable(booktabs = TRUE, align = "lrrrrr",
        caption = "Model 2 (corrected). Home-field advantage is highly significant.") %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = "HOLD_position", font_size = 10)
```

```{r effect-sizes, echo=FALSE}
b0 <- coef(m_full)[1]
b1 <- coef(m_full)[2]

hfa_prob     <- plogis(b0)
hfa_prob_lo  <- plogis(ci_full[1, 1])
hfa_prob_hi  <- plogis(ci_full[1, 2])
hfa_elo_pts  <- b0 / b1
odds_100     <- exp(b1 * 100)
odds_1pt_pct <- (exp(b1) - 1) * 100

mcfadden <- 1 - as.numeric(
  logLik(m_full) / logLik(glm(home_win ~ 1, data = games_home, family = binomial))
)
```

### Interpretation

**Home-field advantage ($\beta_0$ = `r sprintf("%.4f", b0)`).** Between evenly rated
teams, the home side wins
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * hfa_prob)` of the time
(95% CI `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100*hfa_prob_lo)`--`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100*hfa_prob_hi)`).
Playing at home multiplies the odds of winning by `r sprintf("%.3f", exp(b0))`. Dividing
$\beta_0$ by $\beta_1$ converts this into Elo units: home field is worth about
**`r sprintf("%.0f", hfa_elo_pts)` Elo points**, comparable to a meaningful gap in team
quality.

**Elo difference ($\beta_1$ = `r sprintf("%.6f", b1)`).** Each additional Elo point
raises the odds of winning by `r sprintf("%.3f%%", odds_1pt_pct)`. A 100-point Elo edge
multiplies the odds by `r sprintf("%.3f", odds_100)`, a
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", (odds_100 - 1) * 100)` increase.

**Fit.** McFadden's pseudo-$R^2$ is `r sprintf("%.4f", mcfadden)`. This is low in
absolute terms but unremarkable for game-level sports prediction, where outcomes are
genuinely close to coin flips. It is a reason to be modest about the model, not a sign
that it is broken.

```{r fig-winprob, fig.height=3.8, fig.cap="Fitted win probability with a 95\\% confidence ribbon. The gap between the curve and the 50\\% line at zero Elo difference is the home-field advantage."}
nd <- tibble(elo_diff = seq(-350, 350, by = 5))
lp <- predict(m_full, newdata = nd, type = "link", se.fit = TRUE)
nd <- nd %>%
  mutate(fit = plogis(lp$fit),
         lo  = plogis(lp$fit - 1.96 * lp$se.fit),
         hi  = plogis(lp$fit + 1.96 * lp$se.fit))

ggplot(nd, aes(elo_diff, fit)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, colour = grey, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = grey, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = navy, alpha = 0.18) +
  geom_line(colour = navy, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(data = binned, aes(mid, rate, size = n),
             colour = accent, alpha = 0.75, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 4, guide = "none") +
  annotate("segment", x = 0, xend = 0, y = 0.5, yend = hfa_prob,
           colour = accent, linewidth = 0.9,
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.16, "cm"), ends = "both")) +
  annotate("text", x = 18, y = (0.5 + hfa_prob) / 2, hjust = 0, size = 3.2,
           colour = accent, fontface = "bold",
           label = sprintf("Home edge:\n%.1f%% at equal Elo", 100 * hfa_prob)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1), limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(title = "Win probability rises smoothly with Elo advantage",
       subtitle = "Fitted logistic curve; red points are observed win rates per 50-point bin",
       x = "Elo difference (home \u2212 away)", y = "P(home win)",
       caption = "Ribbon shows the 95% confidence interval for the fitted probability.")
```

# Out-of-sample validation

The earlier draft evaluated the model on the same games used to fit it. That
overstates performance and, for calibration specifically, is close to meaningless. We
therefore split by season: train on 2000--2016 and test on 2017--2021.

```{r train-test}
train <- games_home %>% filter(season <= 2016)
test  <- games_home %>% filter(season >= 2017)

m_train <- glm(home_win ~ elo_diff, data = train, family = binomial)

p_train <- predict(m_train, type = "response")
p_test  <- predict(m_train, newdata = test, type = "response")
```

```{r perf, echo=FALSE}
roc_tr <- roc(train$home_win, p_train, quiet = TRUE)
roc_te <- roc(test$home_win,  p_test,  quiet = TRUE)

auc_tr <- as.numeric(auc(roc_tr))
auc_te <- as.numeric(auc(roc_te))

acc_te  <- mean((p_test > 0.5) == test$home_win)
base_te <- mean(test$home_win)

tibble(
  Metric = c("Games", "AUC", "Accuracy at 0.5 threshold",
             "Brier score", "Baseline: always pick home"),
  Train  = c(format(nrow(train), big.mark = ","),
             sprintf("%.4f", auc_tr),
             sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * mean((p_train > 0.5) == train$home_win)),
             sprintf("%.4f", mean((p_train - train$home_win)^2)),
             sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * mean(train$home_win))),
  Test   = c(format(nrow(test), big.mark = ","),
             sprintf("%.4f", auc_te),
             sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * acc_te),
             sprintf("%.4f", mean((p_test - test$home_win)^2)),
             sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * base_te))
) %>%
  kable(booktabs = TRUE, align = "lrr",
        caption = "Performance on training (2000-2016) and held-out (2017-2021) seasons.") %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = "HOLD_position", font_size = 10)
```

Test AUC of `r sprintf("%.3f", auc_te)` is essentially identical to the training figure
of `r sprintf("%.3f", auc_tr)`, so the model is not overfitting. It beats the
always-pick-the-home-team baseline by
`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * (acc_te - base_te))` percentage points of accuracy.

```{r fig-roc, fig.height=3.9, fig.cap="ROC curves on training and held-out seasons are nearly indistinguishable, indicating the model generalises."}
roc_frame <- function(obj, label) {
  tibble(fpr = 1 - obj$specificities,
         tpr = obj$sensitivities,
         Set = label) %>%
    arrange(fpr, tpr)
}

bind_rows(roc_frame(roc_tr, sprintf("Train 2000-2016 (AUC %.3f)", auc_tr)),
          roc_frame(roc_te, sprintf("Test 2017-2021 (AUC %.3f)",  auc_te))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(fpr, tpr, colour = Set)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = grey, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(navy, accent)) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(title = "The model generalises to unseen seasons",
       subtitle = "ROC curves, home-win classification",
       x = "False positive rate", y = "True positive rate", colour = NULL)
```

## Calibration: why the in-sample plot was misleading

A logistic model with an intercept is calibrated on its training data *by
construction* --- the score equations force predicted and observed totals to match
exactly. Plotting in-sample calibration therefore cannot tell us whether the model is
any good.

```{r calib-identity}
# The fitting procedure guarantees this equality; it is not evidence of model quality.
c(predicted_wins = sum(fitted(m_full)), actual_wins = sum(games_home$home_win))
```

The honest test is calibration on seasons the model has never seen.

```{r fig-calibration, fig.height=4.0, fig.cap="In-sample calibration is guaranteed to look good. On held-out seasons the model systematically over-predicts home wins."}
calib <- function(p, y, label) {
  tibble(p = p, y = y) %>%
    mutate(bin = cut(p, breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.1), include.lowest = TRUE)) %>%
    group_by(bin) %>%
    filter(n() >= 10) %>%
    summarise(n = n(), pred = mean(p), wins = sum(y), .groups = "drop") %>%
    mutate(actual = wins / n, Set = label) %>%
    bind_cols(wilson_ci(.$wins, .$n))
}

calib_all <- bind_rows(
  calib(fitted(m_full), games_home$home_win, "In-sample (all games)"),
  calib(p_test,         test$home_win,       "Held-out (2017-2021)")
) %>%
  mutate(Set = factor(Set, levels = c("In-sample (all games)", "Held-out (2017-2021)")))

gap_in  <- calib_all %>% filter(Set == "In-sample (all games)")  %>% summarise(g = mean(abs(actual - pred))) %>% pull(g)
gap_out <- calib_all %>% filter(Set == "Held-out (2017-2021)")   %>% summarise(g = mean(abs(actual - pred))) %>% pull(g)

ggplot(calib_all, aes(pred, actual)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = accent, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), width = 0, colour = grey, linewidth = 0.45) +
  geom_line(colour = navy, linewidth = 0.6, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_point(aes(size = n), colour = navy) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 4.5, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  facet_wrap(~ Set) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0.1, 1), ylim = c(0.1, 1)) +
  labs(title = "Calibration must be judged out of sample",
       subtitle = "Predicted vs observed home win rate, decile bins with 95% Wilson intervals",
       x = "Predicted probability", y = "Observed win rate",
       caption = "Points below the dashed line mean the model predicted more home wins than occurred.")
```

Mean absolute calibration error rises from `r sprintf("%.3f", gap_in)` in sample to
`r sprintf("%.3f", gap_out)` out of sample. The held-out points sit almost uniformly
*below* the diagonal: the model predicts home wins at a rate of
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * mean(p_test))` but observes only
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * mean(test$home_win))`, an over-prediction of
`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * (mean(p_test) - mean(test$home_win)))` percentage points.

This is not random error. It is directional, and the next section explains why.

# Home-field advantage over time

If home advantage were stable, a model trained on 2000--2016 would not systematically
over-predict home wins later. We estimate the advantage separately for each season.

```{r hfa-by-season}
hfa_season <- games_home %>%
  group_by(season) %>%
  group_modify(~ {
    fit <- glm(home_win ~ elo_diff, data = .x, family = binomial)
    cf  <- summary(fit)$coefficients
    tibble(n = nrow(.x), est = cf[1, 1], se = cf[1, 2])
  }) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(prob = plogis(est),
         lo   = plogis(est - 1.96 * se),
         hi   = plogis(est + 1.96 * se))
```

```{r fig-hfa, fig.height=4.3, fig.cap="Season-by-season home-field advantage at equal Elo. The edge is stable near 58\\% for two decades, then falls to a coin flip from 2019 onward."}
trend <- lm(prob ~ season, data = hfa_season)
slope_pp <- coef(trend)[2] * 100

ggplot(hfa_season, aes(season, prob)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 2018.5, xmax = 2021.5, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = sand, alpha = 0.22) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, colour = "grey40", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = navy, alpha = 0.13) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = accent,
              linewidth = 0.7, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(colour = navy, linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(colour = navy, size = 1.9) +
  annotate("text", x = 2020, y = 0.70, size = 3.1, colour = "grey25",
           fontface = "bold", label = "2019-2021") +
  annotate("text", x = 2020, y = 0.675, size = 2.8, colour = "grey35",
           label = "2020 played to\nempty stadiums") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2000, 2020, 4)) +
  labs(title = "Home-field advantage did not fade gradually \u2014 it fell off a cliff",
       subtitle = "Modelled home win probability between evenly rated teams, by season",
       x = NULL, y = "P(home win) at equal Elo",
       caption = sprintf("Ribbon is the 95%% CI per season. Dashed red line is the linear trend (%.2f pp per year).", slope_pp))
```

```{r era-model}
games_home <- games_home %>%
  mutate(era = case_when(
    season <= 2018 ~ "2000-2018",
    season == 2019 ~ "2019",
    season == 2020 ~ "2020 (no crowds)",
    TRUE           ~ "2021"
  ) %>% factor(levels = c("2000-2018", "2019", "2020 (no crowds)", "2021")))

m_era <- glm(home_win ~ elo_diff + era, data = games_home, family = binomial)
lrt   <- anova(m_full, m_era, test = "Chisq")
```

```{r era-table, echo=FALSE}
be <- coef(m_era)
eras <- levels(games_home$era)
lp <- c(be[1], be[1] + be["era2019"], be[1] + be["era2020 (no crowds)"], be[1] + be["era2021"])

tibble(
  Era = eras,
  Games = as.integer(table(games_home$era)),
  `P(home win) at equal Elo` = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * plogis(lp)),
  `Change vs 2000-2018` = c("--", sprintf("%+.1f pp", 100 * (plogis(lp[-1]) - plogis(lp[1]))))
) %>%
  mutate(Games = format(Games, big.mark = ",")) %>%
  kable(booktabs = TRUE, align = "lrrr",
        caption = "Home-field advantage by era, from a single model with era indicators.") %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = "HOLD_position", font_size = 10) %>%
  row_spec(3, bold = TRUE)
```

Adding era indicators improves fit significantly (likelihood-ratio
$\chi^2 = `r sprintf("%.2f", lrt$Deviance[2])`$ on `r lrt$Df[2]` df,
$p = `r sprintf("%.4f", lrt[["Pr(>Chi)"]][2])`$). Home advantage was
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * plogis(lp[1]))` through 2018 and
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * plogis(lp[3]))` in 2020 --- below even money.

The 2020 season is the most striking single data point, and it has an obvious candidate
explanation: pandemic restrictions meant most games were played without spectators. We
must be careful here. This is observational, 2020 differed in other ways (disrupted
preparation, no preseason, altered travel), and the decline had already begun in 2019
before any crowd restrictions. The crowd hypothesis is consistent with the data but not
established by it.

# Conclusion

Team strength dominates. A 100-point Elo advantage multiplies the odds of winning by
`r sprintf("%.2f", odds_100)`, and Elo difference alone yields an out-of-sample AUC of
`r sprintf("%.3f", auc_te)`.

Home-field advantage is real and substantial, contrary to our earlier draft. Over
2000--2021 the home team won `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * hfa_prob)` of games between
evenly rated opponents --- an edge worth roughly `r sprintf("%.0f", hfa_elo_pts)` Elo
points and significant at $p < 10^{-23}$. The earlier null result came from contrasting
home games with `r n_neutral` neutral-site games rather than estimating the advantage
from the intercept.

That advantage is not constant. It held near 58% through 2018 and then fell to roughly
even from 2019 to 2021. Any model trained on the older regime will over-predict home
teams going forward, which is exactly the miscalibration we measured.

The methodological lesson generalises: the original specification was not a coding
error. It ran cleanly, produced plausible output and a coherent narrative. It was wrong
because the coefficient did not mean what it appeared to mean. Checking what a
comparison group actually contains --- 61 games, in this case --- matters more than
checking that the code executes.

# Limitations

1. **Elo is an imperfect summary of strength.** It omits injuries, weather, coaching and
   roster churn. FiveThirtyEight's quarterback-adjusted ratings (`qbelo`) are in the
   file and would likely improve the model.
2. **Only one predictor.** Rest days, travel distance, divisional matchups, altitude and
   betting lines are all excluded.
3. **Home advantage is treated as league-wide.** In reality it varies by stadium; Denver
   and Seattle are not Jacksonville. A hierarchical model with team-level random effects
   would capture this.
4. **Games are treated as independent.** Outcomes within a season share teams, so the
   standard errors are mildly optimistic.
5. **The 2020 interpretation is not causal.** Crowd absence is one of several things
   that changed that year.
6. **Coverage ends in 2021.** FiveThirtyEight retired the dataset, so we cannot see
   whether home advantage recovered once crowds returned.

# Reproducibility

Place `nfl_elo.csv` beside this file and knit. All figures and every number quoted in
the text are computed at knit time from the data; none are typed in by hand.

```{r session, echo=FALSE}
si <- sessionInfo()
tibble(
  Component = c("R version", "Platform", "Key packages"),
  Value = c(
    si$R.version$version.string,
    si$R.version$platform,
    paste(sprintf("%s %s", c("dplyr", "ggplot2", "pROC"),
                  c(as.character(packageVersion("dplyr")),
                    as.character(packageVersion("ggplot2")),
                    as.character(packageVersion("pROC")))),
          collapse = ", ")
  )
) %>%
  kable(booktabs = TRUE, align = "ll", caption = "Session information.") %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = "HOLD_position", font_size = 9)
```
